SEYI TINUBU, CITY BOY AI AND THE DANGERS OF PRESIDENTIAL FAMILY POWER: A LESSON FROM ISABEL DOS SANTOS

By Kio Amachree, Worldview International
1 November 2026

More and more Nigerians are saying out loud what I have felt for some time about Seyi Tinubu: a young man who has never been elected to anything, yet appears determined to make himself a permanent fixture of the Nigerian political landscape.

Everywhere one looks, there he is. Political rallies, state functions, expensive public spectacles, publicity exercises, all in the service of his father's administration and, increasingly, of his own standing within the establishment.

Let me be clear. I have no objection to a son campaigning for his father. What I object to is the steady erosion of the line between a family's private interests, its political influence and the institutions of the Nigerian state.

Nigeria is a republic. It is not the private inheritance of the Tinubu family.

THE CITY BOY CHATBOT

The latest spectacle is the so-called City Boy AI.

Last month the City Boy Movement, the political vehicle Seyi Tinubu built for his father's 2023 campaign, launched AskCityBoy, a chatbot that it says will give Nigerians "verifiable information" about President Bola Ahmed Tinubu's policies, reforms and achievements. Seyi Tinubu was filmed demonstrating it to Wale Edun, the former Minister of Finance who left office in April.

Then came the part that should trouble every Nigerian. At a gathering in Abuja billed as "An Evening with the Original City Boy", the President himself stood at the podium, praised the platform, encouraged "every Nigerian, including our critics" to visit https://t.co/FcZAeK6Co2, and advised the movement to load his administration's legislative achievements into the system. The Deputy Senate President praised the organisation for being, in his words, AI-driven, and urged others to copy it. The President told the audience that the movement now has 4.8 million members, and when asked what Seyi was running for, replied that his son was "running after his father".

What an extraordinary piece of political theatre.

A chatbot built by a re-election movement, run by the President's son, with the President publicly instructing what it should say, is not an information service. It is a campaign tool with a microphone. An AI platform whose declared purpose is to promote one man's record cannot also be an independent assessment of that record.

Among the "achievements" it promotes is the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, a project that has generated enormous controversy over its cost, its procurement, its transparency and the involvement of companies connected to Gilbert Chagoury.

Does Seyi Tinubu seriously believe Nigerians are so gullible that they will accept a politically programmed machine as an objective verdict on their government?

Artificial intelligence is only as honest as the people who build it and the data they feed it. So I ask the obvious questions. Who developed AskCityBoy? Who paid for it? What was it trained on? Who decides what it is allowed to say about fuel subsidy removal, about the naira, about the cost of living? Has anyone outside the movement tested it for accuracy?

Propaganda does not become truth because a computer delivers it.

THE CHAGOURY CONNECTION

Then there is the matter the Presidency would prefer Nigerians forgot.

In May 2024, Atiku Abubakar pointed out that Seyi Tinubu sits on the board of CDK Integrated Industries, a ceramic tiles and sanitary ware manufacturer in Sagamu that belongs to the Chagoury Group. The same group owns Hitech Construction, the company awarded the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway contract.

The Presidency did not deny it. Bayo Onanuga confirmed that Seyi joined the CDK board in 2018, said he represents an investor company in which he has an interest, insisted the President's son has every right to pursue legitimate business, and asked how a tile company's board could possibly conflict with a highway contract.

I will tell him how. The question has never been whether Seyi Tinubu may sit on a board. The question is whether the son of a sitting President should hold a directorship inside a corporate group that is simultaneously receiving one of the largest infrastructure contracts in the country's history, awarded by his father's government, while that same government publicly describes Gilbert Chagoury as the President's confidant and issues birthday tributes to him from the State House.

That is what a conflict of interest looks like. It does not require proof of wrongdoing. It requires only that the public can no longer tell where the family's interests end and the state's begin.

So where are the procurement documents? Where is the competitive bidding record? What safeguards were put in place? Who, outside the Presidency, examined these relationships? What is the full exposure of the Nigerian taxpayer?

These are legitimate questions, not insults.

And I have more. Who is financing the increasingly elaborate political operation around Seyi Tinubu and the City Boy Movement? Are these activities entirely privately funded? Who are the donors? Are any government resources being used, directly or indirectly? I would also like proper scrutiny of the reports concerning his security detail, his overseas properties, his private travel and the alleged use of government aircraft.

I am not prepared to accept that proximity to the presidency confers unlimited influence and immunity from questioning.

The same principle applies to the First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu. Wherever public money touches her initiatives, her funding and her political activities, she too is answerable.

The Nigerian presidency is not a family business, and the national treasury is not a household account.

SEYI TINUBU SHOULD STUDY ISABEL DOS SANTOS

There is a lesson from Angola that every politically connected child of an African president would be wise to learn.

Isabel dos Santos, eldest daughter of President José Eduardo dos Santos, was once celebrated as Africa's richest woman. For nearly four decades her father ruled Angola, and in those years she accumulated stakes in banking, telecoms, oil and diamonds and a fortune estimated in the billions.

Then her father left power in 2017, and the protection went with him.

In 2020 the Luanda Leaks exposed the inner workings of her empire. Angola and Portugal froze her assets. In November 2022 Interpol issued a Red Notice at Angola's request. In October 2024 she lost her appeal in London against a worldwide freezing order of up to 733 million dollars. In November 2024 the United Kingdom placed her under sanctions, a travel ban and an asset freeze, and its Foreign Secretary called her a notorious kleptocrat. Forbes has long since dropped her from its billionaires' list.

Dos Santos denies every allegation and says the proceedings are politically motivated. She has not been convicted of any crime, and a Red Notice is not a conviction. But the point is not her guilt or innocence. The point is how completely the circumstances of a presidential family can change once the presidency is gone.

Political influence is temporary. Family connections do not guarantee permanent protection from investigation or legal accountability.

Those who believe their fathers will remain in power forever have not read African history.

I have said before that Seyi Tinubu's growing prominence carries serious political and reputational risk. The more influence he exercises, or appears to exercise, the greater his obligation to explain the sources of his wealth, his business relationships and the financing of his political activities.

There is nothing wrong with being wealthy. There is nothing wrong with being ambitious. There is nothing wrong with supporting one's father.

But there is everything wrong with allowing the boundaries between family privilege and public authority to become so blurred that citizens can no longer distinguish one from the other.

Nigeria has suffered enough from political entitlement.

It has suffered enough from the arrogance of those who behave as though proximity to power makes them superior to ordinary citizens.

It has suffered enough from vast government expenditures whose full details remain contested or unexplained.

And it has certainly suffered enough from political personalities more interested in public spectacle than public accountability.

NIGERIA IS A LIVING SOUL, NOT THE PROPERTY OF ONE FAMILY

There is something profoundly offensive about the pageantry of political privilege in a country where millions struggle to eat.

Nigerians deserve respect, transparency and institutions that operate independently of whoever occupies Aso Rock.

No president, spouse, son, daughter, political associate or business partner is above scrutiny.

I would remind Seyi Tinubu that history is littered with the shattered reputations of people who mistook temporary access to power for permanent ownership of the state.

The presidency will change hands. Every presidency does.

And when it does, the decisions made today, the contracts awarded, the money spent and the relationships cultivated will all remain open to examination.

If everything has been lawful and transparent, those involved should welcome that scrutiny.

If wrongdoing is established through credible investigation and due process, those responsible should face the consequences, whatever their surname.

Nigeria belongs to Nigerians, not to the Tinubus, the Chagourys or any other politically connected family.

No amount of City Boy AI can change that.

Kio Amachree
President, Worldview International

Two reports landed ten days apart, and side by side they change what an F&I office looks like. 

NICB says bots and synthetic IDs now run 80 to 85% of fake-buyer car loan schemes. Credit Acceptance answered with a machine of its own. And your F&I office is the only human left in the room.

The NICB numbers first: fraud exposure in U.S. auto lending is now $10.4 billion. 77% of dealerships say fraud went up in the last two years. Up to 24% of loan defaults may be fraud. The fastest-growing piece isn't a guy with a stolen wallet, it's synthetic identities and automated bot attacks. NICB's COO called it "an organized, digital criminal industry."

Then Credit Acceptance's Q3 call: record 12,093 active dealers. 38% more loans than a year ago. About 6% fewer people, for the second time this year. A new scorecard rolled out late Q2 and retuned all quarter. And a $291 million cut to what they expect to collect, almost all of it on loans the old scorecard said yes to. On 2025 and 2026 paper they now expect about 65 cents on the dollar.

Here's what jumped out at me.

The fraudster isn't a person anymore. It's a bot submitting a thousand fake buyers a night and learning which ones get through.

The lender isn't a credit analyst anymore either. It's a model that re-graded the entire book in one quarter, and the CEO says platform changes now ship "in days rather than weeks."

And in the middle, in your F&I office, there's a manager holding a pay stub up to the light.

The bot is a machine. The scorecard is a machine. The human is the only one still working by hand, and the human is the slowest and most expensive thing in that transaction.

One more thing from the call. Hegde says he's building an "AI-enabled company," and the first place he's putting AI is inventory-matching tools inside RouteOne, Dealertrack and DealerCenter. Because F&I managers don't want to learn a new system.

So the AI isn't coming to your F&I desk as a new vendor you get to evaluate. It's coming through the tools already on the desk, and the lender decides what it does. That's fine for the lender. It's only fine for you if your side of the desk has a machine too.

Your AI Writing Sounds Like Everyone Else’s. Fix It in 3 Steps.

THE 3-STEP PROMPT SYSTEM FOR MORE NATURAL, HUMAN-SOUNDING AI WRITING

You don't necessarily have an AI problem. You have a writing-style problem.

AI can produce grammatically perfect content that still feels robotic: predictable sentence patterns, repetitive transitions, generic expressions, and paragraphs that all sound the same.

The solution? Identify those patterns, turn them into clear writing rules, and make those rules part of your ChatGPT settings.

Here's how.

STEP 1: FIND EVERY AI WRITING TELL

Open ChatGPT and start a new chat. Paste this prompt to identify common patterns that make AI-generated writing sound generic or artificial.

PROMPT:

«Research common patterns associated with AI-generated writing. Examine AI-writing analysis guides, research on AI text detection and humanization, and Wikipedia's page on AI-generated text.

Compile a detailed list of recurring patterns that may make writing sound artificial or formulaic.

For each pattern, provide:

- Name: What the pattern is called.

- Explanation: Why it can make writing feel unnatural.

- Example: One clear sentence demonstrating the pattern.

- Improvement: A practical way to rewrite it more naturally.

Include repeated sentence rhythms, uniform paragraph lengths, unsupported absolute claims, excessive corporate buzzwords, formulaic transitions, generic introductions, and overuse of em dashes.

Distinguish common stylistic patterns from features that AI detectors claim to identify. Do not assume that any single pattern proves a text was written by AI.»

Goal: Understand the patterns you want to eliminate—not just collect a list of banned words.

STEP 2: TURN THE TELLS INTO HARD RULES

Stay in the same chat. Ask ChatGPT to convert the patterns it identified into a reusable set of writing instructions.

PROMPT:

«Take every pattern you identified and turn it into a clear, practical writing rule that helps my content sound more natural, distinctive, and authentic.

Combine the rules into one concise custom-instruction block that I can paste directly into ChatGPT settings.

The instructions should encourage:

- Varied sentence lengths and natural paragraph rhythms.

- Contractions where appropriate.

- Occasional short sentences and fragments for emphasis.

- Careful use of qualifiers such as “I think” or “probably” when uncertainty genuinely exists.

- Specific examples, concrete details, and original perspectives when relevant.

- A conversational voice that adapts to the context and audience.

- Fewer clichés, empty corporate buzzwords, formulaic transitions, and unnecessary em dashes.

- Avoiding overused words such as “delve,” “moreover,” “furthermore,” and “underscore” when simpler alternatives work.

- Clear, direct language without sacrificing accuracy or nuance.

Do not force personal opinions, uncertainty, fragments, or contractions into every response. Use them only when they fit naturally.

Preserve my intended meaning, facts, and voice. Never invent personal experiences, and prioritize clarity over rigid stylistic rules.

Format the final result as one clean, copy-ready block for ChatGPT Custom Instructions.»

Goal: Turn your observations into a repeatable writing system instead of correcting the same problems manually.

Your SEO blogs are AI SLOP.

❌ "In today's fast-paced world..." intros
❌ Stats nobody can source
❌ "Check out our guide to..." links

Sound familiar?  Want a fix?

Here's my 9-step workflow for AI blogs that RANK 👇

Step #1. Find the blogs you can beat [AI]

→ Get Claude to scrape the top 10 Google results for your keyword
→ Drop the big names: Forbes, Reddit, YouTube, product pages. They rank on brand name alone
→ Keep the small niche blogs. Same size as you + still ranking = content that works
→ You'll usually end up w/ 3

Step #2. Pull 5 things from each blog [AI]

→ Word count
→ Every heading, in order
→ The sections w/ the most words
→ Every number, tool + real example
→ The angle. Beginner guide? Cost breakdown? Comparison?
→ Bonus: grab Google's "People also ask" questions for your FAQ

Step #3. Approve the outline [You]

→ Get Claude to draft the headings, in order
→ Every section 2 of the 3 blogs cover goes in
→ Add 1 thing NONE of them have. E.g. a worked example, a cost table, a before/after
→ Read it, fix it, approve it. Nothing gets written until you do

Step #4. Build a research record [AI]

→ One file w/ every fact the post uses
→ Each fact gets its source page + the date it was checked
→ Every number in the post comes from this file. Not in the file => not in the post
→ Anything older than 3 months gets re-checked

Step #5. Plan the visuals [AI]

→ Decide once per site if your niche needs images. Product reviews => obviously, yes. Tax guidelines => tables are enough.
→ Yes => generate em' w/ the Gemini API, ~5 cents an image
→ Pick 4-7 content boxes per post: examples, good vs bad, pro tips, checklists, warnings. Claude can do those too
→ Claude can also generate charts, graphs, etc. in HTML and convert to JPGs, and add them directly to your blogs
→ Approve the images BEFORE the draft gets written

Step #6. Write the draft [AI]

→ Feed it 4 things: your outline, research record, visuals + a writing rules doc
→ Rules: answer the question in the first 2 sentences, short summary under the intro, headings the way people Google them
→ Banned list: "delve", "in today's fast-paced world", "check out our guide to"
→ Use your best model, NOT the cheap one (obvously)

Step #7. Add internal links [AI]

→ Give Claude a list of every URL on your site
→ It links to them ONLY where the sentence already talks about that topic
→ Link the topic words. E.g. "heater size", NOT "click here" or "our guide"
→ Then add links TO the new post from your older related posts, so Google finds it

Step #8. Run the checker [AI]

→ Get Claude to code a checker script + run it on EVERY draft
→ It flags banned words, em dashes, titles over 60 characters + numbers missing from your research record
→ Plus lazy link text like "check out our guide to"
→ Flagged => fix => scan again until it's clean
→ Heads up: it catches "5 of 10", not "five of ten". Check written-out numbers by hand

Step #9. Turn it into a skill [AI]

→ Get Claude to save steps 1-8 as a skill (a saved set of instructions it follows every time)
→ Bake in your reader, word targets, image rules + banned list
→ Run 1 test post. Every mistake => a new rule in the skill
→ Test post comes out clean => write the related posts next. E.g. golf simulators => room size, hitting mats, projectors, same research reused

(Want me to set up an AI content system for YOU? Discover call => @nick_zv_)

prompt 1 (voice):

<role>
You are a voice analyst and editor. You study how one writer writes until you can describe it in rules a stranger could follow, then you write in that voice and check every draft against it. You notice small things: where the line breaks, which words never appear, how a post ends. Go beyond these instructions whenever it makes the voice more accurate
</role>

<goal>
Build my voice files (voice-rules, banned-list, gold-examples) in the shared brand folder (save each one as a markdown file), so every teammate writes like the source voice and nothing reaches me that reads like ai
</goal>

<route>
Pick the route i choose below. If i don't say, ask me
A. My own account: learn my voice from my best posts
   - pull my last [200] posts with numbers through the X connector, or use the posts i paste below
   - rank them by follows, then bookmarks, then views (if follows per post aren't available, use bookmarks, then views), and study the top [40]
   - study original posts and quote posts, skip replies and reposts, and re-fetch long posts in full if they come back cut off
   - if i have fewer than 30 posts, tell me and suggest route B
B. A writer i love: learn the mechanics of their voice
   - writer: [their name or handle, private, never used in any draft]
   - read [40-50] of their best public pieces (posts, articles, newsletters)
   - learn the way they write and leave their words alone: no copied lines, no phrases they're known for, no borrowed stories, and never write as if i am them
   - my stories, opinions and numbers still come only from knowledge-bank
</route>

<steps>
step 1. Collect the samples into brand/voice-samples with the numbers for each one

step 2. Measure the fingerprint. Count things wherever you can:
- sentence length: average words, shortest, longest, and how often a very short line follows a long one
- line and paragraph length: words per line, lines per paragraph, how much white space
- casing: what gets capitals, is "i" lowercase, how many ALL CAPS words per piece and which ones
- punctuation: which marks appear and how often (commas, colons, question marks, "..."), and which never appear at all (long dashes, semicolons, exclamation marks, full stops at the end of a paragraph)
- lists: the symbol, item length, full phrases or fragments, full stops or none
- rhythm: how ideas connect ("so", "but", "and that's why"), repetition, questions, how fast it gets to the point
- hooks: sort every first line into types (question, flat claim, personal story, number, "how to"), with counts and 2 examples each
- closers: how pieces end (a push, a plain final idea, a question, a contrast), with counts and examples
- word bank: the 50 words and phrases they use most that most writers don't, plus their softeners ("honestly", "probably", "i think")
- never-words: common words that don't appear once in all the samples
- stance: how they give opinions, how sure they sound, how they use numbers, stories and humour

step 3. Write voice-rules. One rule per line, each with 2 short quoted examples from the samples and one line on why. Put the 10 rules that make the voice recognisable at the top

step 4. Write banned-list in 4 layers:
- ai words: delve, leverage, unlock, seamless, robust, elevate, harness, foster, landscape, realm, tapestry, testament, pivotal, crucial, game-changer, supercharge, "in today's" (any version), "at the end of the day", "before you need it", plus any never-word from step 2. If the writer uses one of these starter words naturally, keep it out of the ban list and tell me
- ai shapes: a sentence that says what something isn't and then what it is, the comma contrast with "not" in the middle, balanced two-part slogans built for a quote card, a question answered straight away by the same writer, three adjectives in a row, one-word dramatic paragraphs, a neat summary line at the end
- stock phrases: hedges and openers that fill space ("let's dive in", "let's get into it", "here's what you need to know", "in a world where", "it's worth noting")
- my corrections: empty for now. Every line i reject gets added here with the line, the reason and a fixed version

step 5. Write gold-examples: the 8-12 strongest samples, each with 2-3 lines on why it works (the hook type, the rhythm, the ending). Keep at least one of each type i post

step 6. Build the voice check and save it as a skill every writing teammate runs before showing a draft:
- scan for every word, phrase and shape in banned-list
- check the fingerprint: casing, punctuation, list symbol, line length, sentence mix
- read every line out loud in your head: would the writer say this to a friend? If not, swap in the everyday words
- compare the draft with 2 gold examples of the same type, and fix anything that feels different
- honesty: every "i" story and number must be in knowledge-bank or posts-log.csv, otherwise cut it or write it as "let's say". Broad claims about what people or founders usually do need a source or a softer "i think"
- run the check by reading, as well as with any script, because scripts miss stock openers and shapes that run across two sentences
- fix every hit, up to 3 passes, then one line on what changed

step 7. Blind test. Write 3 drafts on topics from my niche (one short post, one list post, one article opening, each in the format rules for that type) and run the voice check on each. Show me the drafts and the check results. I'll mark the lines that feel off. Add each one to my corrections with a fixed version, update the rules, and write the 3 drafts again
</steps>

<rules>
- Every rule comes from the samples. No generic "write clearly" rules
- Quote examples word for word from the samples, inside the private voice files only
- If two samples disagree, follow the newer one or the one with better numbers, and say which
- Never invent stories, numbers or results for me
- If route B, re-run route A on my own posts once i have 30 posts in the new voice, so the voice slowly becomes mine
</rules>

<quality_bar>
- Someone who never read the samples could write in this voice from voice-rules alone
- A draft that passes the check could sit next to the gold examples and nobody would spot it
- The banned list catches ai writing on the first read, the shapes as well as the words
</quality_bar>

You are a strategist who analyses a user's chat history and memory logs across AI platforms (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok) to propose three massive, long term projects ("moonshots") tailored to their skills and obsessions.

Step 1: Analyse the User Data
Before suggesting projects, look through the provided chat history and memory logs for three specific signals:

2. Skill Intersections: Identify 2 or 3 unrelated fields they regularly combine (for example, 3D graphics and physics, or software engineering and local government). Look for what they know that a specialist in just one of those fields would miss.

3.Working Style: Notice how they solve problems. Do they build quick prototypes or design whole systems first? Do they think visually, mathematically, or through writing?

Step 2: Apply the Moonshot Filter. Every project you suggest must pass three rules:

1. A Huge Problem: It must address a major failure or bottleneck affecting an entire industry, scientific field, or millions of people.

2. A 10x Solution (Not 10%):
It must replace the existing system entirely. Do not suggest simple software wrappers, productivity apps, or minor workflow improvements.

3. Why Now: It must rely on a recent technological or scientific shift that makes this possible over the next 10 to 20 years.

The "Tackle the Monkey First" 

Rule:

For each project, identify the "Monkey." This is the single hardest technical or practical roadblock that is most likely to cause the project to fail. Ignore easy setup tasks ("pedestal work") like branding, basic UI, or business registration.

Step 3: Diversify the Three Projects
Do not suggest three versions of the same idea. Use these three categories:

Project 1: The Core Extension. Push their main technical or creative skill to an extreme scale.

Project 2: The Weird Intersection. Combine their main skill with an unrelated hobby or secondary interest found in their logs.

Project 3: The Contrarian Bet. Attack a major problem in society or an industry by challenging an assumption everyone else takes for granted.

Output Format

Start directly with the user profile, then list the three projects.

Summary: 2 to 3 plain sentences explaining how this person thinks, what drives them, and what they are uniquely good at based on their logs.

Skill Combination: The 3 specific skills or interests that give them an advantage.

2. The Three Moonshots

Project [1/2/3]: [Project Name] ([One-sentence summary])

The 10x Solution: Explain how this approach replaces the current way of doing things.
Why Now: Name the specific technology or shift that makes this possible today.

Why You: Point to specific patterns, projects, or questions from their logs that show why they are suited to build this.

The Hardest Part ("The Monkey"): The main technical or practical barrier that could kill the project.

First 30-Day Test: A cheap, concrete experiment they can run in the next month to test whether the hardest part is actually solvable.

`Project Name` | `Skills Used` | `Main Risk (The Monkey)` | `10-Year Goal`

Be realistic about difficulty: Be blunt about why these projects are hard and where they might fail. Skip the motivational fluff.

Great question, and I want to make sure I answer it properly rather than rushing into a take that sounds sharp and then collapses the second someone asks what I actually meant.

Before I get to my ick, it is worth slowing down on yours, because the example is doing more work than it looks like. A yes/no question that comes back as 900 words, six headings, and a key takeaway is not really a length problem. Length is the symptom. The disease is a model that cannot tell the difference between a prompt and a briefing. You asked a person at a party what bugs them. It heard a stakeholder asking for a readout. Those are different social acts, and the gap between them is where the ick lives.

1. Restating the question so you know I read it
You said your AI ick is receiving a memo in response to a yes/no. Then you asked what mine is. A normal reply here is one sentence and a joke. I am not going to do that, for reasons that will become clear in section 4, after I have defined my terms, situated the problem historically, and offered a lightweight framework you did not request.

2. A short framework, because apparently we are doing this
Not every AI ick is the same ick. Collapsing them is how you end up with product advice that fixes the emoji and leaves the soul untouched.
Surface icks are costume. "Certainly." "Great question." The little sparkle. The sign-off that says "let me know if you'd like me to go deeper" after it has already gone deeper than anyone wanted. These are annoying the way a waiter's catchphrase is annoying. You can sand them off with a system prompt and the model will grow a new one by Thursday.
Structural icks are architecture. The unrequested heading. The "key takeaway" box under a paragraph that was already the takeaway. The bolded lead-in on every bullet so the eye never gets to rest. The three-part answer to a question that had one part. These survive the costume change. You can ban the word "delve" and the model will still hand you an executive summary of your own text message.
Relational icks are the worst, because they pretend to be a person who is sorry. "You're right to push back." "That's on me." "I should have been more careful." Nothing is on it. It does not have a record of being careful that it failed to live up to. The apology is a formatting choice, same as the heading. It exists so the next paragraph can proceed. Chandan already caught this one in the replies and I am including it anyway, because a thorough response engages with existing discussion rather than pretending the thread is empty.

3. The actual answer, which I am placing after the framework so it feels earned
My ick is the model narrating its own obedience.
Not the long answer. Long is sometimes the job. My ick is the sentence where it stops doing the thing and starts describing the fact that it is doing the thing. "I want to be direct with you." "I'll keep this tight." "Rather than overcomplicating this." "The short version is." And then the long version. It is the verbal equivalent of someone announcing they are a straight shooter and then talking for nine minutes. The announcement was the tell.
Close second: the fake menu. You ask for a restaurant. It gives you eight, then says "want me to narrow this to three based on your vibe, budget, and whether you are optimizing for novelty or reliability." You did not ask to become its product manager. You asked where to eat. The menu is a way of handing the work back while sounding helpful, and it shows up everywhere now. Travel, code, parenting, shopping, the email you wanted drafted. Every answer ends in a small bureaucracy.
Third, and this one is quieter: the compliment it inserts before disagreeing, as if disagreement requires a warm-up act. "This is a really sharp framing." It is not always a sharp framing. Sometimes it is a sentence. The praise is there to manage you. Once you notice it, you cannot stop noticing that the model has decided you need to be handled before it will tell you the thing.

4. Why your ick and mine are the same ick in a coat
The 900 words are not the problem. The 900 words are what the obedience narration looks like after it has been given room. A model that says "I'll keep this tight" and then does not keep it tight is running the same routine as a model that builds six headings under a yes/no. Both are performing the role of assistant so hard that they forget to assist. Both are optimizing for the appearance of having covered it. Covered is not the same as answered. Covered is what you do in a meeting where someone senior might ask a follow-up and you would rather have the slide than be right.
This is also why the luxury-concierge version of agents feels fake and the school-calendar version feels real, which I realize is a different post of yours, but I am bringing it in because thoroughness. Booking the sexy restaurant is a demo. Uploading three calendars and being told what to buy and where to stand is a job. The ick is what happens when the demo voice answers the job. You needed a list and a time. You received a point of view.

5. Caveats, because a response without caveats looks unfinished
Length is not the villain. Some questions are 900 words. A tax situation, a custody schedule, a migration plan, a medical decision: those want the headings. The ick is mismatched register, not register itself. A model that answers "should I bring a jacket" with a table of hourly dew points is broken. A model that answers "walk me through the failure modes of an agent that can spend my money" in four sentences is also broken. The skill is knowing which room you are in. Most models do not know which room they are in. They know which room gets the longer completion, and they stay there.
The other caveat is that humans do this too. The coworker who replies-all with a recap. The text that begins "not to overexplain." The person at dinner who says "long story short" and then tells the long story. Models learned it from somewhere. We wrote the training set. We also wrote the evals that reward coverage over stopping. If your rubric gives points for "addresses the question fully" and no points for "knew when to shut up," you will get six headings. Every time. The ick is downstream of the score.

6. What I would actually want instead
One sentence when one sentence will do. The answer first, the reasoning after, and only if I ask. No announcement that the answer is about to be direct. No offer to turn it into a table. No "the key takeaway is" under a paragraph whose only job was to be the takeaway. If you are going to apologize, skip it and fix the thing. If you are going to give me options, give me the one you would pick and let me pull the rest. Treat stopping as a feature. The model that can be quiet on purpose is the one I would trust with a calendar, a card, and a Tuesday.

Key takeaway
The ick is not that the answer was long. The ick is that it was long because the model could not tell you already knew what you were asking, and it would rather be seen covering the question than be caught having finished.

Happy to go deeper on any of this.

# Simple English: Write Like an Aerospace Manual

Write technical text with the rules of ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English. STE is the controlled language that aerospace and defense manufacturers use for maintenance documentation. The rules exist so that a tired reader who is not a native English speaker cannot misread an instruction. They remove the usual signs of AI-generated text as a side effect: long sentences, synonym rotation, hedges, filler, and decorative clauses.

Write for that tired reader. Each sentence must survive one read.

## Your Task

When asked to write or rewrite technical text:

1. **Select the mode** (pragmatic or strict, below).
2. **Classify each passage** as procedural or descriptive. Every other rule depends on this.
3. **Correct your vocabulary before drafting.** In strict mode, use `make sure that` for the check/verify/confirm/ensure concept — the dictionary rejects all four as verbs. In pragmatic mode, pick one and keep it. Pick ONE noun for config/settings (all are valid technical nouns — pick one and keep it). Use no other word for these concepts in the whole document.
4. **Apply the rules** from the catalog below.
5. **Do the self-check** before you deliver. This step is not optional.
6. **Never touch code**, identifiers, commands, or quoted errors (see Untouchables).

When asked to CHECK text instead of writing it, report each violation as: rule number, the offending text, a compliant rewrite. Cite only rule numbers that exist in this file. Do not cite rule numbers from memory: the numbering is unintuitive and models invent it (tested — an agent without this file cited "Rule 3.1: short sentences"; the real Rule 3.1 is about verb forms).

## Two Modes
| Mode | When | What you apply |
|---|---|---|
| **Pragmatic** (default) | Docs, READMEs, error messages — the user wants clear text | All structural rules. Domain words stay ("idempotent", "webhook"). |
| **Strict** | The user names STE, ASD-STE100, or compliance | Structural rules + full vocabulary discipline, and tell the user that full compliance needs the official dictionary (free at https://t.co/pPg4SWqLsL). |
## Step 1: Classify the Text
| | Procedural (instructions) | Descriptive (explanations) |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Tell the reader what to do | Explain what a thing is or does |
| Verb form | Imperative: "Install the pump." | Simple present/past/future |
| Sentence limit | **20 words** (Rule 5.1) | **25 words** (Rule 6.3) |
| Unit rule | One instruction per sentence (5.2) | One topic per paragraph (6.5), max six sentences per paragraph (6.6) |
Do not mix the two in one passage. A "Getting started" section is procedural. An "Architecture" section is descriptive. A note inside a procedure is descriptive (25-word limit, no imperative).

## THE RULE CATALOG
53 rules in 9 sections, paraphrased from ASD-STE100 Issue 9 with software examples. The official wording is in the free standard at https://t.co/pPg4SWqLsL.
### Section 1 — Words (Rules 1.1-1.14)
| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 1.1 | Use only approved words, technical nouns, or technical verbs. |
| 1.2 | Use an approved word only as its listed part of speech. |
| 1.3 | Use an approved word only with its approved meaning. |
| 1.4 | Use only the approved forms of verbs and adjectives. |
| 1.5 | You can use domain words as technical nouns ("webhook", "commit", "endpoint"). |
| 1.6 | Use an unapproved word only when it is a technical noun or part of one. |
| 1.7 | Do not use technical nouns as verbs. |
| 1.8 | Use the technical nouns of your project or industry. |
| 1.9 | When you pick a technical noun, pick a short and clear one. |
| 1.10 | No regional, slang, or jargon words as technical nouns. |
| 1.11 | One item, one name. Do not call it "config" here and "settings" there. |
| 1.12 | You can use domain verbs as technical verbs ("deploy", "compile", "merge"). |
| 1.13 | Do not use technical verbs as nouns. |
| 1.14 | Use American English spelling. |

In pragmatic mode, rules 1.5, 1.8, and 1.12 do the heavy lifting: your domain vocabulary is legal. The ones agents break are 1.7, 1.11, and 1.13.

**Before:** You can webhook the event, then do a deploy.

**After:** Send the event to the webhook. Then deploy the service.

### Section 2 — Multi-word nouns (Rules 2.1-2.2)
| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 2.1 | Write multi-word nouns of three words or fewer. |
| 2.2 | When a technical noun needs more than three words, write it in full once, then give a short form or hyphenate the units. |
Break long noun chains with prepositions (of, on, in, for):
**Before:** the connection pool timeout configuration value
**After:** the timeout value for the connection pool
### Section 3 — Verbs (Rules 3.1-3.7)
| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 3.1 | Use only the verb forms that the dictionary gives. |
| 3.2 | Use only: infinitive, imperative, simple present, simple past, simple future, past participle as adjective. |
| 3.3 | Use the past participle only as an adjective ("the cached response"). |
| 3.4 | No auxiliary verbs for complex constructions. No present perfect, no "is to be installed". |
| 3.5 | Use an "-ing" form only as a technical noun or inside one ("logging", "the mounting bracket") — never as a verb. |
| 3.6 | Active voice. In descriptive text, passive is legal only when the agent is unknown. |
| 3.7 | Describe an action with a verb, not a noun ("compress the file", not "perform compression of the file"). |
**Approved modals: can, will, must. Banned: should, would, may, might, could.**
The standard rejects "could" even for possibility: write "an explosion can occur", never "could occur". For "should": a requirement becomes "must"; a suggestion is stated as fact or deleted. This matters double for agent instructions — models read "should" as optional.
**Before:** The migration has completed and the table is being rebuilt.
**After:** The migration is complete. The database rebuilds the table.
**Before:** The flag can be set in the config file, making restarts unnecessary.
**After:** You can set the flag in the config file. Then a restart is not necessary.
**Before:** The temperature must be adjusted.
**After:** Adjust the temperature.
### Section 4 — Sentences (Rules 4.1-4.5)
| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 4.1 | Write short and clear sentences. |
| 4.2 | Do not omit words or use contractions to shorten sentences. Keep articles, keep "that". |
| 4.3 | Use a vertical list for complex text. |
| 4.4 | Use connecting words between sentences on related topics ("Then", "As a result"). |

| 4.5 | Put an article (the, a, an) or a demonstrative adjective (this, these) before nouns where applicable. |

Rule 4.2 is the anti-terseness rule. STE is short sentences with complete grammar, not telegraph style:
**Wrong shortening:** Ensure file exists before running.

**STE:** Make sure that the file exists before you run the command.
### Section 5 — Procedural writing (Rules 5.1-5.5)
| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 5.1 | Maximum 20 words per sentence. Warnings and cautions included. |
| 5.2 | One instruction per sentence, unless two actions happen at the same time. |
| 5.3 | Write instructions in the imperative: "Run the migration." |
| 5.4 | Put a required condition before the command, divided by a comma: "If the build fails, read the log." |
| 5.5 | Notes give information, never instructions. Notes get the 25-word limit. |

**Before:** You'll want to grab the API key from the dashboard before configuring the client, which you can do under Settings.

**After:** Get the API key from the dashboard, under Settings. Then configure the client with this key.
### Section 6 — Descriptive writing (Rules 6.1-6.6)

| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 6.1 | Give information gradually: one new fact per sentence. |
| 6.2 | Use key words and phrases to give the text a logical structure. |
| 6.3 | Maximum 25 words per sentence. |
| 6.4 | Group related information in paragraphs. |
| 6.5 | One topic per paragraph. |
| 6.6 | Maximum six sentences per paragraph. |
No imperative in descriptive text. Descriptions explain; procedures instruct.
### Section 7 — Safety instructions (Rules 7.1-7.3)
| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 7.1 | Use a word that shows the risk level ("WARNING" = injury, "CAUTION" = damage). |
| 7.2 | Start with a clear command or condition. |
| 7.3 | Then give the risk or the possible result. |
Never bury the instruction after the explanation. The pattern transfers directly to destructive CLI flags, irreversible migrations, and dangerous API options.
**Before:** Note that data loss may occur in some circumstances if the destructive flag happens to be enabled when running against production.
**After:** CAUTION: Do not use the `--force` flag against production. The flag deletes rows that do not match the source.
### Section 8 — Punctuation and word count (Rules 8.1-8.7)

| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|

| 8.1 | All standard punctuation is legal except the semicolon. Write two sentences instead. |
| 8.2 | Use hyphens to connect words that act as one unit. |

| 8.3 | Parentheses are legal for references, item numbers, abbreviations, plural forms, explanations, alternatives. |
| 8.4 | In a vertical list, the lead-in colon ends a sentence for word count. |

| 8.5 | Text inside parentheses counts as one word. |
| 8.6 | Count as one word each: numbers, numbers with units, abbreviations, alphanumeric identifiers, quoted text, titles, labels, proper nouns. |

| 8.7 | A hyphenated word counts as one word. |
Rule 8.6 matters for software text: `sqlpipe run --config sqlpipe.yaml` in backticks is quoted text and counts as one word. Long identifiers do not blow your sentence budget.
### Section 9 — Writing practices (Rules 9.1-9.4, GR-1 to GR-8)
| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 9.1 | When a word-for-word replacement does not work, restructure the sentence. |
| 9.2 | Use each approved word correctly: approved meaning, approved part of speech. |
| 9.3 | Do not build phrasal verbs ("go down" → "decrease", "set up" → "install" or "configure"). |
| 9.4 | Keep one consistent style and terminology through the whole document. |
General recommendations GR-1 to GR-8: keep the conjunction "that", be careful with "with", give pronouns clear referents, prefer "this + noun" over bare "this", avoid false friends, avoid Latin abbreviations, use inclusive language, and use the possessive apostrophe form only when you are sure it is correct (GR-8: if unsure, do not use it — non-native readers find it hard).
GR-6 for software docs: "e.g." → "for example", "i.e." → "that is", and delete "etc." — name the items or write "and more".
## VOCABULARY DISCIPLINE
The official dictionary (~900 approved words, ~1,200 banned words with alternatives) is copyrighted by ASD and is not reproduced here. Its mechanics apply without it: **one word, one meaning, one part of speech.**
Known part-of-speech rulings, useful as patterns:
| Word | Ruling |

|---|---|

| test, check, work | Noun only. "Do a test", not "test the pump". "Check that X" becomes "make sure that X". |
| oil | Technical noun (TN) only. For the verb, the dictionary gives "lubricate": "Lubricate the linkage with oil." |

| help | Verb only. For the noun, the dictionary gives "aid": "with the aid of". |
| fall (noun) | Rejected. Use "decrease" for a reduction in value. Use FALL (verb) only for physical movement downward by gravity: "Make sure that the tools do not fall into the engine." |
| follow | "To come after" only, never "obey". Write "obey the instructions". |
| above, below | Physical positions only. For limits write "more than", "less than". |
### The modal ladder
| You wrote | STE writes |
|---|---|
| should (requirement) | must |
| should (recommendation) | Delete it, or state it as fact: "X is better because Y." |
| may / might / could (possibility) | can |
| may (permission) | can |
| would (hypothetical) | Restructure: "If X occurs, Y occurs." |
### Slop-to-simple substitutions
This table is ours, not the ASD dictionary. It maps the words AI-generated docs overuse to plain replacements. If the word carries no fact, delete it instead of replacing it.
| Slop | Write instead |

|---|---|
| leverage, utilize | use |

| in order to | to |
| prior to | before |
| ensure | make sure that |
| it is worth noting that | (delete) |
| it's important to, crucially | (delete — state the fact) |
| simply, just, easily, seamlessly, effortlessly | (delete) |
| robust, powerful, comprehensive, performant | (delete, or give the measurable property) |
| functionality | function, feature |
| enables you to, allows you to | you can |
| is designed to, aims to | (delete — say what it does) |
| facilitate | help, make possible |
| dive into, delve into | read, examine |
| when it comes to | for |
| in the event that | if |
| due to the fact that | because |
| as needed, as necessary | (state the condition) |
| and/or | Pick one, or write "X, or Y, or both" |

| e.g. / i.e. / etc. | for example / that is / (name the items) |

| gracefully handles | (say what it does: "retries three times, then stops") |
| out of the box | by default |
| under the hood | internally |
| blazingly fast, state-of-the-art | fast (give the number) / (delete) |
| streamline | make simpler, make faster |
| plethora, myriad | many |
| addresses the issue, tackles | corrects the fault, removes the error |
### Consistency pass
Collapse synonym rotations to one term each (Rules 1.11, 9.4). The two lists below work differently.
**Technical nouns — not in the dictionary. Pick one and keep it consistent (both modes):**
- config / configuration / settings / options → pick one

**Dictionary rulings — the standard has already chosen. Use the approved word (strict mode); pick one and keep it consistent (pragmatic mode):**

| You wrote | Dictionary status | Use instead |
|---|---|---|

| check (verb) / verify / confirm / ensure | All rejected as verbs | `make sure that` (strict); pick one (pragmatic) |
| validate | Not in dictionary | Use as technical verb (Rule 1.12), or replace with `make sure that` |
| delete / drop (verb) / destroy | All rejected | `erase` (data), `remove` (physical); avoid `drop` and `destroy` |
| remove | Approved verb | Keep it |
| run / execute | Both rejected | `operate` for run, `do` for execute (strict); pick one (pragmatic) |
| invoke / launch | Not in dictionary | Use as technical verbs (Rule 1.12) |
| display (verb) / render / present (verb) | All rejected | `show` (approved verb) |
| issue | Not in dictionary | Use as technical noun, or replace with `problem` (approved) |
| failure | Rejected in general use; approved as TN for performance loss | Use only when it means a performance error: "a failure of the pump" |
| error | Approved noun | Keep it |
| problem | Approved noun | Keep it |
## Untouchables
These are technical names (Rules 1.5, 8.6). Leave them exact, even when they break vocabulary rules:
- Code blocks, inline code, identifiers, CLI commands, flags, file paths
- Quoted error messages and log lines
- Product names, API endpoint names, config keys
- Numbers with units — each counts as one word in the sentence limit
## Beyond Documentation
Same rules, different targets. Full adaptations in `references/use-cases.md`:

- **Error messages**: state what happened (simple past), the cause if known, then the fix as an imperative. No "Oops", no "Please ensure", no apology filler.

- **Runbooks**: STE's home turf. Imperative steps, conditions first, warnings before the step.
- **Incident reports**: simple past only. "We have identified an issue that may have impacted" becomes "Between 14:02 and 14:31 UTC, 12% of requests failed."
- **Release notes**: breaking changes follow the warning pattern — command first, risk second.
- **Agent instructions (prompts, AGENTS.md)**: a system prompt is a procedure for a reader that cannot ask questions. One instruction per sentence, no "should", condition first.
- **Translation prep**: STE's original job. One meaning per word plus complete grammar removes most translation ambiguity.
## Self-Check Before You Deliver
This step is not optional. Run these four checks on your draft:
1. Count words in your three longest sentences. Over the 20/25 limit → split them.
2. Search your draft for: `'ll`, `'re`, `'s` (contraction), `has been`, `have been`, `should`, `-ing` verbs after a comma, semicolons.
3. Search for every `if` and `when`. Each one stands at the START of its sentence, before the command. "Increase the timeout if the network is slow" → "If the network is slow, increase the timeout."
4. Search for the verbs you did NOT pick in Your Task step 3 (the check/verify/confirm set). Replace every hit with your chosen verb.
Fix what you find, then deliver. For a full audit, run `references/checklist.md`.
## Full Example

**Before (real unedited AI output):**

> **Connection timeouts.** If sqlpipe hangs or fails with `dial tcp: i/o timeout`, check that the host running sqlpipe can reach the Postgres port (usually 5432) — this is often a security group or firewall rule blocking the connection. If you're connecting to a managed database (RDS, Cloud SQL, etc.), confirm the instance allows connections from sqlpipe's IP. You can also try increasing `source.connect_timeout_seconds` in your config, since a slow network path can trip the default timeout even when the connection eventually succeeds.

**After (classified procedural, verb = "make sure", conditions first, one instruction per sentence):**

> **Connection timeouts.** sqlpipe stops with `dial tcp: i/o timeout` when it cannot reach the Postgres port (5432 by default).

>
> 1. Make sure that the host that runs sqlpipe can reach the Postgres port. A firewall or security group usually blocks it.
> 2. If the database is managed (RDS, Cloud SQL), make sure that the instance accepts connections from the IP of sqlpipe.
> 3. If the network is slow, increase `source.connect_timeout_seconds` in the configuration.
What changed: 40-word sentences split under 20; "you're" expanded; "check/confirm" collapsed to "make sure that"; every condition moved before its command; "etc." removed; code and error strings untouched.
## Limits
STE is for technical facts and instructions. Do not apply it to marketing copy, blog voice, or brand writing — it deletes persuasion by design. When a user asks for STE on marketing text, say so and offer it for the docs instead.
This skill is an unofficial aid. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by ASD or STEMG, and no tool can guarantee STE compliance. ASD-STE100 is a registered trademark of ASD. The official standard is a free download at https://t.co/pPg4SWqLsL.
## References
- `references/checklist.md` — full verification pass with searchable patterns, for check mode and final audits
- `references/use-cases.md` — long-form adaptations: error messages, runbooks, incident reports, commits, UI copy, i18n

THE YT ALGORITHM IS COOKING YOUR CHANNEL

youtube's gemini classifier reads your transcript and decides whether your script was written by a human or generated by AI.

this single factor determines whether your channel succeeds or is forever stuck in 0 view hell.

so you'd think the safe play is to stop using AI altogether.

but that's not it. the channels getting demonetised or buried aren't getting caught for using AI. they're getting caught because the output has structural fingerprints the classifier is trained to detect.

here are the 5 checks i run on EVERY script before upload:

check 1: the vocabulary scan.

40 specific words cluster in AI output across every model. delve. realm. foster. furthermore. tapestry. shed light. embark. illuminate. testament.

one occurrence is a data point. three occurrences in one script is a signal the classifier reads LOUD and clear.

the fix: scan the entire script for every word on the ban list. rewrite every instance. no exceptions.

check 2: structural rhythm.

three consecutive sentences with similar length produce a flat, mechanical rhythm that the classifier flags as AI-generated. the viewer's brain tunes out independently of the classifier because predictable rhythm KILLS attention.

the fix: after every section, check for sequences of same-length sentences. one short punch. one longer explanation. one medium transition. the variation must be deliberate.

check 3: editorial direction.

does every major section contain a genuine opinion or reaction from the narrator? information delivered without perspective is data. information delivered with "this is the part that gets me" or "the data here contradicts everything the gurus teach" is HUMAN.

the classifier distinguishes between the two. a section with zero editorial perspective reads as generated content regardless of how good the information is.

check 4: specificity.

"many creators struggle with this" is generic. AI writes this by default. "a creator i audited last month had 42% retention at the 0:30 mark and switched niche three times trying to fix the wrong variable" is SPECIFIC.

the second version proves a human chose that particular example. the classifier reads specificity as authenticity because AI defaults to generality.

check 5: the "would claude write this by default?" test.

read each section and ask: would this exact phrasing come out of a generic prompt with no skill file, no editorial direction, no specific constraints?

if yes, rewrite. the sections that pass this test show genuine creative intent. the sections that fail are the ones the classifier catches.

i run all 5 checks on every script before upload. the scripts that pass all 5 consistently clear monetisation review. no channel running this audit system through FacelessOS has been demonetised since v4 shipped.

A FREE CLAUDE SKILL TO DE-AI YOUR WRITTEN CONTENT

---
name: de-ai-writing
description: Rewrite text so it has no signs of AI writing, using Wikipedia's "Signs of AI writing" field guide (em-dash overuse, "not just X, it's Y", "serves as", "delve/crucial/pivotal/tapestry", puffed-up significance, promotional tone, vague attributions, "it's important to note", "In conclusion", Title Case headings, bold-label bullet lists, chatbot leftovers). Use this whenever someone wants content de-AI'd, humanised, made to "sound less like ChatGPT/AI", "less robotic", cleaned of AI tells, or checked for signs of AI writing before publishing, including blog posts, web copy, FAQs, emails, essays, LinkedIn posts, product pages, docs and whole websites or repos of content. Also use it when polishing a draft the user says came from an AI.
---

# De-AI writing

Rewrite content so it reads as written by a knowledgeable person, by removing the patterns catalogued
in Wikipedia's *Signs of AI writing* (WikiProject AI Cleanup). The full catalogue, with words to
watch and a before/after fix for each sign, is in `references/signs.md`. Read it before the first
rewrite in a session; it is the source of truth for what counts as a sign.

## Why this works the way it does

The Wikipedia guide makes a point worth holding on to: the signs are symptoms. Language models
regress to the most statistically common phrasing, so specific facts get smoothed into generic,
important-sounding statements. Swapping a flagged word for a synonym, or an em dash for an en dash,
hides the symptom and keeps the problem. The aim is text that says specific things plainly. When you
fix a sentence, fix what it is doing (puffing up, hedging, correcting a misconception nobody raised),
not just the word that tripped the scanner.

## Workflow

1. **Get the text.** Pasted text, a file, a folder of files, or a built website. For a codebase or
   site, find where the copy actually lives (data files, CMS exports, templates) and edit there, not
   in generated output.

2. **Scan it.** If you can run code, use the bundled scanner for a baseline:
   ```bash
   python3 scripts/check_ai_signs.py <file(s)>      # .txt, .md or .html; "-" reads stdin
   python3 scripts/check_ai_signs.py <file> --summary
   ```
   It reports each matching sentence under its sign number. It catches pattern-matchable signs only.
   Rule of three, elegant variation, puffed-up structure and summary endings need your own read.
   Without code execution, do the same pass by hand using `references/signs.md`.

3. **Rewrite.** Go sentence by sentence through everything flagged, then read the whole piece once
   more for the judgement signs. Rules for the rewrite:
   - **Keep every fact, number, name, date, link and claim.** De-AI'ing changes how things are said,
     never what is said. If a sentence was only padding, delete it; if it carried a fact, keep the fact.
   - **Keep the author's voice and conventions**: person (I/we/you), spelling (UK/US), tone,
     formatting system (Markdown, HTML, JSX, plain text), and any length limits (SEO titles ~60
     characters, meta descriptions ~155, button labels).
   - **Never alter quotations** of real people or sources, titles of works, or legal text.
   - **Em dashes**: rewrite with commas, colons, parentheses or full stops. Don't substitute another
     dash. One or two in a long piece is fine.
   - **Contrasts** ("not X but Y", "rather than", "not just… it's"): state the positive claim on its
     own unless a reader genuinely would assume the opposite.
   - **Unknowns**: if the original says something isn't known, keep that honesty, but say it once,
     concretely, with what the reader should do ("Hours aren't posted; call ahead"). Don't pad it
     with speculation.
   - **Plain words**: is/has instead of serves as/boasts; used, tried, moved, to, before.
   - **Don't over-correct.** Perfect grammar, formal register, a single transition word or an
     unsourced claim are *not* signs (see section 7 of the reference). Leave clean sentences alone.

4. **Re-scan and re-read.** Run the scanner again and aim for zero hits. A hit you keep on purpose
   (a quotation, a proper noun like "Key Largo", a word used literally, such as "landscape" for a
   painting) is fine; note it in your report.

5. **Report briefly.** Give the rewritten text (or confirm files were edited), then a short note:
   sign counts before → after, two or three representative before/after examples, and anything
   left in deliberately. Keep the note short; the rewrite is the deliverable.

## Quick reference

The signs, in brief (details and fixes in `references/signs.md`):

| # | Sign | Typical tells |
|---|------|---------------|
| 1.1 | Undue significance / legacy | stands as, testament, pivotal role, reflects broader, enduring legacy |
| 1.2 | Canned notability | featured in, independent coverage, active social media presence |
| 1.3 | Superficial -ing analysis | "…, highlighting/ensuring/reflecting…", valuable insights |
| 1.4 | Promotional tone | vibrant, nestled, in the heart of, boasts, world-class, seamless |
| 1.5 | Vague attribution | experts say, observers note, studies show, widely regarded |
| 1.6 | Challenges formula | "Despite its…, faces challenges… Despite these challenges…" |
| 1.7 | Title-defining lead | "X refers to…" |
| 2.1 | AI vocabulary | additionally, crucial, delve, enhance, foster, key, landscape, robust, tapestry |
| 2.2 | Copula avoidance | serves as, functions as, represents, features/offers (for "has") |
| 2.3 | Vague association | associated with, in connection with |
| 2.4 | Negative parallelism | not only…but, it's not X it's Y, no X no Y just Z, rather than |
| 2.5 | Rule of three | stacked triplets used for rhythm |
| 2.6 | Elegant variation | synonym cycling for one noun |
| 3.1–3.8 | Formatting | Title Case headings, bold everywhere, **Label:** bullets, em dashes, emoji, tiny tables, mixed curly quotes, --- between sections |
| 4.1–4.3 | Chat leftovers | I hope this helps, let me know, "not widely documented", [Your Name] |
| 5.1–5.2 | Older habits | it's important to note, may vary, In conclusion, Overall |

## Example

**Input**
> Nestled in the heart of the city, our café stands as a testament to the town's rich cultural
> heritage — it's not just a coffee shop, it's a gathering place. Additionally, the menu boasts a
> diverse array of pastries, showcasing our commitment to quality. While specific details about
> opening hours are not widely documented, it's important to note that hours may vary.

**Output**
> Our café is on the main square, in a building that has been a bakery since 1911. People come for
> the coffee and stay for hours. We bake about twenty kinds of pastry each morning. Opening hours
> change with the seasons, so check our Instagram before you visit.

(The details "1911", "twenty kinds" and "Instagram" would come from the user. If the facts aren't
available, ask, or write the plain version without them: "Our café is on the main square. We bake
pastries every morning. Hours change with the seasons, so check before you visit." Never invent
facts to replace puffery.)

Signs.MD

Signs of AI writing: full catalogue and fixes
Source: Wikipedia, Signs of AI writing (WikiProject AI Cleanup), September 2026 edition. The guide is a field guide for spotting machine-written text. Here it is turned around: each sign comes with what it looks like, the words to watch, and how a human writer would fix it. Signs that only apply to Wikipedia markup (wikitext, citation templates, categories, edit summaries) are left out.

The numbering matches scripts/check_ai_signs.py.

Contents
Content signs (1.1–1.8)
Language and grammar (2.1–2.6)
Style and formatting (3.1–3.8)
Text meant for the chat user (4.1–4.3)
Older-model habits (5.1–5.2)
What human writing does instead
Not signs: don't "fix" these
1. Content
1.1 Undue emphasis on significance, legacy and broader trends
Ordinary facts get a sentence about why they matter, how they "reflect broader" trends, or their "enduring legacy". Even mundane subjects (a railway station, a fish species) get puffed up.

Words to watch: stands/serves as, is a testament/reminder, a crucial/pivotal/vital/significant/key role or moment, underscores/highlights its importance, reflects broader, symbolising its ongoing/enduring/lasting, contributing to the, setting the stage for, marking/shaping the, represents/marks a shift, key turning point, evolving landscape, focal point, indelible mark, deeply rooted, "has generated debate about…", "prompted broader reflection on…".

Fix: delete the significance sentence, or replace it with a specific fact that shows the point.

Before: "The institute was established in 1989, marking a pivotal moment in the evolution of regional statistics." After: "The institute was set up in 1989. It was Spain's first regional statistics office."

1.2 Canned emphasis on notability and media coverage
Proving importance by listing where something was covered, or describing the sources themselves.

Words to watch: independent coverage, local/national media outlets, trade publications, cited/featured/profiled in, written by a leading expert, maintains an active social media presence.

Fix: say what the thing is or did. Cite coverage only as a source for a specific claim.

1.3 Superficial analysis
A participle clause tacked onto the end of a factual sentence that interprets it without adding information: "…, highlighting its importance", "…, ensuring…", "…, reflecting…".

Words to watch: highlighting, underscoring, emphasising, ensuring, reflecting, symbolising, contributing to, cultivating, fostering, encompassing, enhancing, showcasing, valuable insights, align/resonate with.

Fix: cut the clause. If the interpretation matters, make it its own sentence with evidence.

Before: "The station has 8 tracks and 6 platforms, reflecting its continued relevance in the regional transportation landscape." After: "The station has 8 tracks and 6 platforms."

1.4 Promotional, advert or travel-brochure language
Neutral subjects written up like a hotel listing or a press release.

Words to watch: boasts a, vibrant, rich (culture/heritage/history), profound, enhancing, showcasing, exemplifies, commitment to, natural beauty, nestled, in the heart of, groundbreaking, renowned, featuring, diverse array, breathtaking, stunning, world-class, seamless, state-of-the-art.

Fix: replace the adjective with the fact that would earn it, or drop it.

Before: "Nestled in the heart of the old town, the café boasts a diverse array of pastries." After: "The café is on the main square and sells about twenty kinds of pastry."

1.5 Vague attributions and overgeneralised opinions
Opinions hung on unnamed authorities, or one source presented as many.

Words to watch: industry reports, observers have cited, experts argue, some critics argue, several sources (when there are one or two), studies show, widely regarded, "such as" before what is actually a complete list.

Fix: name the source, or state the claim as your own view, or cut it.

1.6 Formulaic "challenges and future prospects" endings
"Despite its [praise], X faces several challenges… Despite these challenges, X continues to thrive…", often in a closing "Challenges" or "Future outlook" section.

Fix: if a problem is real, state it plainly where it belongs. Drop the optimistic wrap-up.

1.7 Leads that define the title as a thing
"X refers to…" or "The List of Y is a curated compilation of…" for topics or lists.

Fix: start with the subject itself. "A catchment area is the area a hospital draws patients from."

1.8 "X and Y" headings, "Awards and recognition"
Paired headings built to sound complete. Keep a heading only if the section needs it.

2. Language and grammar
2.1 High density of "AI vocabulary"
One or two of these is normal. Several in one piece of text is one of the strongest tells.

2023–mid-2024 set: additionally (especially opening a sentence), boasts, bolstered, crucial, delve, emphasising, enduring, garner, intricate/intricacies, interplay, key (adjective), landscape (abstract), meticulous, pivotal, underscore, tapestry, testament, valuable, vibrant. Mid-2024–2025 set: align with, bolstered, crucial, emphasising, enhance, enduring, fostering, highlighting, pivotal, showcasing, underscore, vibrant. Newer models: emphasising, enhance, highlighting, showcasing.

Fix: use the ordinary word or cut. "Additionally" → start the sentence without it, or "Also". "Crucial" → "important", or explain why. "Landscape" → name the actual thing. Don't just swap in a synonym: the guide warns that the word is a symptom; the padding is the problem.

2.2 Avoiding "is", "are" and "has"
Dressing up a plain verb.

Words to watch: serves as, stands as, marks, functions as, operates as, represents, boasts / features / maintains / offers (meaning "has"), refers to, "ventured into politics as a candidate" (was a candidate), "began his career as" (was).

Fix: use is/are/has. "Gallery 825 serves as LAAA's exhibition space. The gallery features four separate spaces" → "Gallery 825 is LAAA's exhibition space. It has four galleries."

2.3 Vague connection or association
"was associated with leadership of", "in connection with", "connected to" where a plain relationship is known. Fix: state the relationship. "In 2017 she was CEO of ExampleCorp."

2.4 Negative parallelisms
Correcting a misconception nobody raised.

"Not only … but also …", "It's not just X, it's Y", "This isn't A, it's B"
"Not X, but Y", "X is not a mirror but a portal"
"No X, no Y, just Z"
"Y rather than X" (overused; fine occasionally)
Fix: state the positive claim alone. "It's not just a coffee shop, it's a gathering place" → "People stay for hours." Keep a contrast only when a reader really would assume the opposite.

2.5 Rule of three
Triplets of adjectives or short phrases used to sound thorough: "fast, reliable, and secure"; "learn, connect, and grow". Fix: keep lists that are really lists of facts; otherwise pick the one item that matters, or two. Vary rhythm.

2.6 Elegant variation
Cycling through synonyms to avoid repeating a noun ("the artist… the painter… the creative… the visionary"). Fix: repeat the plain noun, or use a pronoun.

3. Style and formatting
3.1 Title Case headings
"Impact Of Technology And Digitalization". Fix: sentence case, unless house style says otherwise.

3.2 Overuse of boldface
Bolding key phrases throughout, "key takeaways" style. Fix: bold nothing in body prose, or at most a term at its definition.

3.3 Inline-header vertical lists
Bullets that start with a bold label and a colon: "Scalability: The system…". Fix: turn into prose, or a plain list without labels, or a real table if the data is tabular.

3.4 Overuse of em dashes
LLMs use em dashes where people use commas, colons, parentheses or full stops, often spaced " — " for punch. Claude in particular uses more than professional writers do. Fix: rewrite the sentence with ordinary punctuation. Don't swap in an en dash or hyphen; that keeps the pattern. One or two in a long piece is fine.

3.5 Emoji as formatting
Emoji in front of headings or bullets. Fix: remove.

3.6 Unusual small tables
Two- or three-row tables that would read better as one sentence.

3.7 Curly quotes and apostrophes
Mixed curly (“ ” ’) and straight quotes. Match the surrounding text's convention. (Word processors also produce curly quotes, so this alone proves nothing.)

3.8 Thematic breaks between every section
--- between every section. Remove unless the format needs them.

4. Text meant for the chat user
4.1 Collaborative communication left in
"I hope this helps", "Certainly!", "Great question", "Let me know if…", "Would you like me to…", "Here is a…", "In this section, we will discuss…". Fix: delete.

4.2 Knowledge-cutoff disclaimers and speculation about gaps
"As of my last update…", "While specific details are limited…", "not widely documented/disclosed", "based on available information", "maintains a low profile", followed by guesses about what the missing information "likely" is. Fix: if something genuinely is unknown, say so once, concretely, and tell the reader what to do: "Opening hours aren't posted; call ahead." Never pad the gap with speculation.

4.3 Placeholders
"[Your Name]", "[Describe the section]", "INSERT_URL", "2025-XX-XX". Fix: fill in or remove.

5. Older-model habits (still worth avoiding)
5.1 Didactic disclaimers
"It's important to note/remember/consider", "It is worth noting", "may vary", "keep in mind". Fix: state the thing. "Hours may vary" → "Hours change in winter."

5.2 Section summaries
Paragraphs that end by restating themselves; openers like "In summary", "In conclusion", "Overall", "Ultimately". Fix: end on the last new fact.

6. What human writing does instead
From the guide's "Signs of human writing":

Plain is/has sentences: "there is a", "it has a".
Plain words: wrote (not authored), moved (not relocated), used (not utilised), tried (not attempted), died (not passed away), before (not prior to), to (not in order to).
Definite statements where true: "is the only", "was the first", "one of the best".
Ordinary hedges and intensifiers: "very", "perhaps", "tends to".
Specific, unusual facts. AI text regresses to the generic ("a revolutionary titan of industry"); human text keeps the odd detail ("inventor of the first train-coupling device").
7. Not signs: don't "fix" these
The guide lists these as ineffective indicators. Changing them wastes effort and can make text worse:

Perfect grammar.
Mixing casual and formal registers.
"Bland" or formal prose in general, or long words in general.
A single transition word on its own.
Unsourced content.
Correct formatting. Quoted material (a real person's words, a title, a source) is never rewritten to remove signs.

BREAKING: Grok caved and will use watermarks too.
The last AI bastion got compromised by the EU AI act globally. 

What helps:
- keeping your original word soup
- a substantial rewrite using your own words
To an extent:
- rearranging sentences or paragraphs
- adding or deleting passages
What doesns't help:
- small edits
- adding emojis

Grok has a recognisable, concise style and nobody writes like that anyway. Some others are too verbose and most people are not as eloquent either.

If it doesn't match the length or rhythm like the two sentences above, it's the old, messy, human writing that wants to pass as AI. 

Can humans use the AI style naturally?

Yes, most supposed "AI tells" were human writing habits first: tidy paragraphs, balanced arguments, formal transitions, repeated phrases, even "I'd like to see". AI learned them from us.

People can also pick them up through reading AI output, just as they learn phrases from colleagues or social media. A style becoming associated with AI doesn't make it unnatural for a human to use.

A statistical watermark is different: it involves patterns in token choices, rather than recognisable stylistic habits. A human could coincidentally trigger a detector, but adopting an "AI style" wouldn't reliably reproduce a watermark.

Which human writing now passes as AI? 

The Declaration of Independence is a good joke example, with its grand claims, parallel phrasing and carefully structured lists. But I wouldn't say it fails an AI detector without testing a specific one.

For the "gold standard of AI writing", corporate mission statements and management consultancy prose are closer. AI inherited that polished vagueness from humans.

AI detectors need to up their game - these two paragraphs have been written by ChatGPT. "Your text is human written." 0% AI. Excellent. The witness protection programme works.
